message.content: Reply with the single word M6B-claude-2
Write a 300-line poem about rivers, numbered lines, no preamble.

content.text:
1. Before the names, before the maps were drawn,
2. the water knew the shape of every valley,
3. pressing its cold thumb into the stone
4. the way a sculptor tests the yielding clay.
5. It did not ask the mountain for permission.
6. It simply leaned, and kept on leaning, downward,
7. a patience older than the oldest trees,
8. a hunger that was not a hunger, only weight.
9. Somewhere high, a single drop let go
10. of a glacier's blue and ancient shoulder,
11. and that was the beginning, if there is one,
12. if anything that moves can claim a start.
13. The drop found another, and the two
14. went looking for a third among the gravel,
15. and soon a thread of silver stitched the moss,
16. and soon the thread was singing to itself.
17. This is how a river learns its voice:
18. by falling, and by falling, and by falling,
19. by striking rock and finding that the rock
20. will hum back, if you strike it long enough.
21. The first rill does not know it is a river.
22. It thinks it is a whisper in the fern,
23. a trembling in the roots of mountain heather,
24. a coldness that the marmot stops to drink.
25. But gravity is a kind of argument
26. that water never tires of agreeing with,
27. and so it gathers, so it braids and doubles,
28. and so the whisper thickens to a word.
29. Below the snowline, where the larches stand
30. like sentries who have long forgotten why,
31. the stream begins to carve its first ravine,
32. a shallow wound that will become a canyon.
33. It takes ten thousand years to cut a foot.
34. It takes a million to unmake a range.
35. The river does not count. It has no clock
36. except the slow pulse of the turning seasons.
37. In spring it swells with everything the winter
38. kept locked in white and silent treasuries,
39. and roars down through the gorges, brown and furious,
40. tearing out the boulders like loose teeth.
41. In summer it grows thin and clear and thoughtful,
42. showing every pebble on its floor,
43. the trout suspended in it like a thought
44. that hasn't quite decided to be spoken.
45. In autumn it is littered with the gold
46. of aspens shaking out their brief inheritance,
47. a currency the current spends at once,
48. carrying each coin away to nowhere.
49. In winter it goes quiet under ice,
50. but listen, kneel, and press your ear to it:
51. beneath the frozen lid it is still going,
52. still muttering its one unending sentence.
53. I have stood beside a river at dawn
54. when mist was lifting off it like a breath,
55. as if the water dreamed all night and woke
56. and exhaled the last remnants of its dreaming.
57. A heron stood there too, one-legged, grave,
58. a gray priest at the altar of the shallows,
59. and neither of us spoke, and neither moved,
60. and the river went on praying for us both.
61. What does a river want? It wants the sea.
62. That is the only answer it has ever given.
63. Every bend, every oxbow, every delay
64. is just the long way round to the same ending.
65. And yet it does not hurry. Look at how
66. it lingers in the meadows, how it loops
67. back on itself as if it had forgotten
68. something on the far side of the field.
69. The meander is the river's way of thinking.
70. It doubles back to reconsider things.
71. It cuts the neck of its own wandering
72. and leaves a crescent lake behind, a memory.
73. Those oxbow lakes go still and green with reeds.
74. The frogs move in. The dragonflies arrive.
75. They are the river's abandoned sentences,
76. the clauses it decided not to finish.
77. Along the banks the willows lean and listen.
78. They have been leaning for a hundred years.
79. Their roots drink deep; their branches trail the surface
80. like fingers of a girl leaned over a boat.
81. The kingfisher, that flash of stolen sky,
82. goes stitching through the shadows like a needle,
83. and where it dives, a ring of light expands
84. and travels out and vanishes downstream.
85. Everything here is traveling downstream:
86. the leaf, the twig, the feather, and the silt,
87. the reflection of the cloud, the cloud itself
88. eventually, returning as the rain.
89. Heraclitus said you cannot step
90. into the same river twice, and he was right,
91. but he forgot to add that you yourself
92. are not the same who stepped in yesterday.
93. Two rivers, then: the water and the wader,
94. both changing, both pretending to stay still,
95. both carrying their sediment of years
96. toward some estuary they can't see.
97. The towns grew up where rivers could be crossed.
98. The fords became the bridges, then the cities.
99. Every capital is kneeling at a river
100. the way a calf kneels down beside its mother.
101. The Thames, the Seine, the Tiber, and the Nile,
102. the Danube threading empires like a rosary,
103. the Ganges where the ashes of the dead
104. drift outward on a current made of prayer.
105. The Mississippi, wide and brown and drowsy,
106. carrying the topsoil of a continent,
107. a whole midwestern farm in every mile,
108. the corn and wheat dissolved into its body.
109. The Amazon, so vast it has no shore
110. that you can see from the middle of its channel,
111. pushing fresh water a hundred miles to sea,
112. as if it would not let the ocean have it.
113. The Yangtze, through its gorges, through its dams,
114. the Mekong feeding half a world of rice,
115. the Volga slow and patient as a grandmother,
116. the Congo dark with forests it has drunk.
117. The Indus, where the oldest cities rose
118. and fell, and left their brickwork in the mud;
119. the Tigris and Euphrates, the first garden,
120. where someone first wrote down a word for water.
121. That word was older than the word for god.
122. Before we prayed, we had to drink. Before
123. we built a temple, we had dug a channel
124. and watched the barley rise along its edges.
125. Irrigation is the oldest poem:
126. a line of water drawn across the dust,
127. and where the line goes, green begins to follow,
128. and where it stops, the desert holds its breath.
129. We have dammed them, we have straightened them,
130. we have poured our poisons in them, made them burn.
131. The Cuyahoga caught fire, and we were shocked
132. that water could forget it was a water.
133. We have lined them up in concrete, buried some
134. beneath the streets, where they still run in darkness,
135. lost rivers flowing under London, under
136. every city, singing in their tunnels.
137. Somewhere under your feet, perhaps, right now,
138. a stream that once had trout and kingfishers
139. is moving through a culvert, blind and patient,
140. remembering the sun it used to hold.
141. And yet they are forgiving, rivers are.
142. Tear out a dam and watch: within a season
143. the salmon find the old way home again,
144. nosing up the gravel that they dreamed of.
145. The salmon are the river's memory.
146. They leave as finger-length and silver children,
147. go out to the enormous salt and wander,
148. and years later, something calls them back.
149. They taste the water, and they know it. Somehow
150. among a thousand tributaries they choose
151. the one that tastes like being born, and climb it,
152. leaping falls, against the whole weight of the world.
153. They do not eat on that last journey. They
154. go red, go hooked of jaw, go ragged-finned,
155. and spawn, and die there in the shallow redds,
156. and give their bodies back to feed the forest.
157. The cedars on those banks are made of salmon.
158. The nitrogen of oceans in their rings.
159. The bear who fishes at the falls is carrying
160. the sea into the mountains in her belly.
161. So the river runs both ways, you see:
162. the water down, the life of it back up,
163. a circulation like the blood's own circuit,
164. the heart of it the ocean, and the veins
165. the creeks and brooks and runnels of the uplands,
166. and we, who live along them, only cells
167. carried a little distance on the current
168. before we, too, are given back as silt.
169. I remember the river of my childhood,
